title: Configuration & Deployment
description: Vulnerabilities arising from insecure defaults, incomplete hardening, improper headers, framework misconfigurations, and proxy/cache behaviors.

attacks.name: Missing security headers
attacks.desc: Failing to deploy browser-hardening HTTP headers (Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options), leaving users vulnerable to downgrade and embedding attacks.
attacks.prevention: Set appropriate HSTS, CSP, frame protection, and content-type headers for each response, then test them in production.

attacks.name: Weak CSP / CSP bypass
attacks.desc: Implementing overly permissive Content Security Policies containing wildcards (*), unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval, or trusted CDNs hosting JSONP endpoints, allowing script injection past policy barriers.
attacks.prevention: Use a restrictive CSP with nonces or hashes, avoid broad sources and unsafe-inline, and review trusted third-party scripts.

attacks.name: Clickjacking / UI redressing
attacks.desc: Overlaying a transparent malicious UI layer over a legitimate application inside an iframe to trick authenticated users into executing unintended privileged clicks or transfers.
attacks.prevention: Deny framing with CSP frame-ancestors unless a specific origin needs it; protect sensitive actions with confirmation where appropriate.

attacks.name: TLS misconfiguration
attacks.desc: Permitting obsolete cryptographic suites (DES, RC4, 3DES) or legacy protocols (SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) vulnerable to cipher downgrade and eavesdropping attacks.
attacks.prevention: Disable obsolete TLS versions and weak ciphers, and use a maintained server configuration with regular scans.

attacks.name: Expired / self-signed cert
attacks.desc: Using expired, self-signed, or improperly signed TLS certificates that degrade cryptographic trust, triggering browser warnings and enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.
attacks.prevention: Automate certificate issuance and renewal, monitor expiry, and install a valid chain from a trusted issuer.

attacks.name: HTTP methods enabled
attacks.desc: Exposing dangerous HTTP verbs (such as PUT allowing arbitrary file creation, DELETE for unauthenticated removal, or TRACE permitting Cross-Site Tracing attacks against cookies).
attacks.prevention: Allow only methods each route needs, and apply the same authentication and authorization checks to every method.

attacks.name: Directory listing enabled
attacks.desc: Leaving web server directory index generation active (e.g. Apache mod_autoindex), allowing visitors to browse arbitrary folders and access source files, backups, and confidential records.
attacks.prevention: Disable directory indexes and serve only intended assets from the document root.

attacks.name: Default credentials
attacks.desc: Deploying commercial software, administrative routers, IoT appliances, or framework dashboards with factory-default usernames and passwords unchanged.
attacks.prevention: Replace factory credentials before deployment, disable unused default accounts, and require unique strong administrator credentials.

attacks.name: Default files exposed
attacks.desc: Leaving sample scripts, environment diagnostics (phpinfo.php), and installation wizards accessible in production, leaking server configuration details and permitting unauthorized re-installation.
attacks.prevention: Remove install, sample, and diagnostic files from production; restrict any necessary diagnostics to trusted operators.

attacks.name: Exposed admin panels
attacks.desc: Allowing public Internet access to administrative interfaces without network-level restrictions, VPN segmentation, or multi-factor authentication requirements.

attacks.name: Debug endpoints exposed
attacks.desc: Failing to restrict developer debugging endpoints (such as Spring Boot /actuator, Symfony /_profiler, or Django debug routes), leaking thread dumps, environment secrets, and memory data.

attacks.name: Verbose errors / stack traces
attacks.desc: Displaying detailed application exception traces, framework versions, database queries, and source code excerpts to end users upon application errors.

attacks.name: CORS misconfiguration
attacks.desc: Configuring Cross-Origin Resource Sharing with reflection of arbitrary Origin headers combined with 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true', enabling cross-site exfiltration of private data.

attacks.name: Cookie attribute flaws
attacks.desc: Issuing session tokens without the Secure flag (permitting cleartext transmission), HttpOnly flag (enabling XSS theft), or SameSite flag (allowing CSRF exploitation).

attacks.name: Cache-control weaknesses
attacks.desc: Failing to set strict Cache-Control directives on authenticated pages, causing intermediate proxies or shared browser histories to store sensitive personal and financial data.

attacks.name: Host header injection
attacks.desc: Manipulating the HTTP Host header in requests to poison dynamically generated links, password reset URLs, cache keys, or internal routing mechanisms.

attacks.name: HTTP request smuggling
attacks.desc: Exploiting discrepancies between front-end reverse proxies and backend application servers in parsing Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers, allowing request hijacking and credential theft.

attacks.name: HTTP response splitting
attacks.desc: Injecting Carriage Return and Line Feed (CRLF) characters into HTTP response headers to split the response into two messages, enabling cache poisoning and XSS.

attacks.name: Web cache poisoning
attacks.desc: Injecting malicious payloads via unkeyed HTTP headers or query parameters that get permanently stored by an intermediate cache and served to unsuspecting subsequent visitors.

attacks.name: Web cache deception
attacks.desc: Tricking an authenticated victim into accessing an endpoint with an appended static file extension (e.g. /account.json/profile.css), causing edge caches to store and expose dynamic private user data.

attacks.name: CDN / WAF misconfiguration
attacks.desc: Failing to firewall direct inbound traffic to the origin web server, allowing attackers to discover the true backend IP address and bypass all CDN and WAF security filters.

attacks.name: WAF fingerprinting & bypass
attacks.desc: Detecting specific Web Application Firewall vendors and employing character encoding, chunked transfer encoding, or payload evasion techniques to slip malicious commands past detection engines.

attacks.name: Open cloud storage buckets
attacks.desc: Leaving AWS S3, Azure Blob, or Google Cloud Storage buckets configured with public read or write access, exposing customer records or allowing arbitrary file tampering.

attacks.name: Git history secrets
attacks.desc: Leaving API keys, passwords, and private certificates in historical git commits even after removing them from the head branch, discoverable via git reflogs and history scrapers.

attacks.name: Framework debug mode
attacks.desc: Running production applications with framework debug flags enabled, rendering interactive error pages with full system environment variables and execution context.

attacks.name: RCE via exposed debug console
attacks.desc: Exploiting interactive developer consoles exposed in production (such as the Werkzeug PIN console or Laravel Ignition facade) to execute arbitrary code directly on the host server.
